claims.text: Strength and deformation behavior in multi-component concentrated alloys are governed by the interaction between lattice distortion and dislocation movement.
Increased lattice distortion impedes dislocation mobility.
Impeded dislocation mobility leads to higher strength.
Impeded dislocation mobility leads to reduced ductility.
Differences in atomic radii and chemical composition produce varying degrees of lattice distortion in MCCAs.
Systematically varying atomic size mismatch and chemical composition will alter lattice distortion in MCCAs.
Room-temperature, quasi-static loading isolates lattice-distortion effects without thermal activation.
Lattice distortion can be characterized by atomic size mismatch and chemical complexity.
Lattice distortion increases the energy barrier for dislocation motion.
A higher energy barrier for dislocation motion enhances strength.
Under identical room-temperature, quasi-static testing conditions, alloys with higher lattice distortion will have higher yield strength than alloys with lower lattice distortion.
Under identical room-temperature, quasi-static testing conditions, alloys with higher lattice distortion will have lower ductility than alloys with lower lattice distortion.
MCCAs containing similarly sized atoms and having simpler chemical compositions provide a minimal-lattice-distortion baseline.
The proposed relationship may not apply under high-temperature or dynamic loading conditions because diffusion or twinning may dominate.
Lattice distortion can be quantified using X-ray diffraction or other structural characterization methods.
Failure to observe both increased yield strength and reduced ductility at higher lattice distortion would falsify the hypothesis.
